claim: Type XVII collagen (COL17) is a transmembrane protein located at the epidermal basement membrane zone.
source: Type XVII collagen (COL17) is a transmembrane protein located at the epidermal basement membrane zone.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as an established fact about COL17.

claim: COL17 deficiency results in premature hair aging phenotypes.
source: COL17 deficiency results in premature hair aging phenotypes and in junctional epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: COL17 deficiency results in junctional epidermolysis bullosa.
source: COL17 deficiency results in premature hair aging phenotypes and in junctional epidermolysis bullosa.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Loss of COL17 leads to transient IFE hypertrophy in neonatal mice owing to aberrant Wnt signaling.
source: Loss of COL17 leads to transient IFE hypertrophy in neonatal mice owing to aberrant Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The replenishment of COL17 in the neonatal epidermis of COL17-null mice reverses the proliferative IFE phenotype and the altered Wnt signaling.
source: The replenishment of COL17 in the neonatal epidermis of COL17-null mice reverses the proliferative IFE phenotype and the altered Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Physical aging abolishes membranous COL17 in IFE basal cells because of inactive atypical protein kinase C signaling.
source: Physical aging abolishes membranous COL17 in IFE basal cells because of inactive atypical protein kinase C signaling and also induces epidermal hyperproliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Physical aging induces epidermal hyperproliferation.
source: Physical aging abolishes membranous COL17 in IFE basal cells because of inactive atypical protein kinase C signaling and also induces epidermal hyperproliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: The overexpression of human COL17 in aged mouse epidermis suppresses IFE hypertrophy.
source: The overexpression of human COL17 in aged mouse epidermis suppresses IFE hypertrophy.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 6.

claim: COL17 governs IFE proliferation of neonatal and aged skin in distinct ways.
source: These findings demonstrate that COL17 governs IFE proliferation of neonatal and aged skin in distinct ways.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: COL17 could be an important target of anti-aging strategies in the skin.
source: Our study indicates that COL17 could be an important target of anti-aging strategies in the skin.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion stated in the abstract based on the findings.

claim: IFE stem cells reside in the basal cell layer.
source: IFE stem cells reside in the basal cell layer; these cells both self-renew and generate the terminally differentiated outer cell layers which function as barriers to the external environment and prevent loss of body fluids (Giangreco et al., 2008; Hsu et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2007; Natsuga, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: IFE stem cells both self-renew and generate the terminally differentiated outer cell layers.
source: IFE stem cells reside in the basal cell layer; these cells both self-renew and generate the terminally differentiated outer cell layers which function as barriers to the external environment and prevent loss of body fluids (Giangreco et al., 2008; Hsu et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2007; Natsuga, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The terminally differentiated outer cell layers function as barriers to the external environment and prevent loss of body fluids.
source: IFE stem cells reside in the basal cell layer; these cells both self-renew and generate the terminally differentiated outer cell layers which function as barriers to the external environment and prevent loss of body fluids (Giangreco et al., 2008; Hsu et al., 2014; Jones et al., 2007; Natsuga, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The heterogeneity of stem cells in organs may be reduced with aging.
source: The relationship between organismal aging and stem cells is an inescapable bond, and the heterogeneity of stem cells in organs may be reduced with aging (Goodell and Rando, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Human skin aging is exemplified by alterations in the dermis and skin appendages, such as the thinning of dermis, dryness, wrinkles, gray hair and hair loss.
source: Human skin aging is exemplified by alterations in the dermis and skin appendages, such as the thinning of dermis, dryness, wrinkles, gray hair and hair loss (Rittié and Fisher, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: The influence of aging on IFE has been controversial.
source: However, the influence of aging on IFE has been controversial.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations showing contradictory results.

claim: Decreased epidermal proliferation has been reported in in vitro and in vivo studies using aged individuals and mice.
source: Although decreased epidermal proliferation has been reported in in vitro and in vivo studies using aged individuals and mice (Giangreco et al., 2008; Gilchrest, 1983; Grove and Kligman, 1983), several recent studies have reported contradictory results, showing sustained and increased proliferation in the aged epidermis (Charruyer et al., 2009; Stern and Bickenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Several recent studies have reported sustained and increased proliferation in the aged epidermis.
source: Although decreased epidermal proliferation has been reported in in vitro and in vivo studies using aged individuals and mice (Giangreco et al., 2008; Gilchrest, 1983; Grove and Kligman, 1983), several recent studies have reported contradictory results, showing sustained and increased proliferation in the aged epidermis (Charruyer et al., 2009; Stern and Bickenbach, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: COL17 is a type II transmembrane protein that is located along the hemidesmosomes in the BMZ.
source: Type XVII collagen (COL17) is a type II transmembrane protein that is located along the hemidesmosomes in the BMZ.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The N-terminus of COL17 is localized in hemidesmosomes, and its extracellular domain reaches the lamina densa.
source: The N-terminus of COL17 is localized in hemidesmosomes, and its extracellular domain reaches the lamina densa (McMillan et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Non-hemidesmosomal COL17 in keratinocytes and human skin has been reported.
source: Non-hemidesmosomal COL17 in keratinocytes and human skin has also been reported (Hirako et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: COL17 has been characterized as a target protein in the autoimmune blistering disease bullous pemphigoid.
source: COL17 has been characterized as a target protein in the autoimmune blistering disease bullous pemphigoid (Nishie, 2014) and also as being the defective protein in junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), a congenital blistering disease (Fine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: COL17 is the defective protein in junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), a congenital blistering disease.
source: COL17 has been characterized as a target protein in the autoimmune blistering disease bullous pemphigoid (Nishie, 2014) and also as being the defective protein in junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB), a congenital blistering disease (Fine et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: COL17 forms a niche for hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs).
source: Recently, COL17 has been shown to form a niche for hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs), as mice lacking the protein and human JEB patients with mutations in COL17A1, the open-reading frame encoding COL17, exhibit a premature aged skin phenotype, including gray hair and hair loss (Matsumura et al., 2016; Nishie et al., 2007; Tanimura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Mice lacking COL17 exhibit a premature aged skin phenotype, including gray hair and hair loss.
source: Recently, COL17 has been shown to form a niche for hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs), as mice lacking the protein and human JEB patients with mutations in COL17A1, the open-reading frame encoding COL17, exhibit a premature aged skin phenotype, including gray hair and hair loss (Matsumura et al., 2016; Nishie et al., 2007; Tanimura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Human JEB patients with mutations in COL17A1 exhibit a premature aged skin phenotype, including gray hair and hair loss.
source: Recently, COL17 has been shown to form a niche for hair follicle stem cells (HFSCs), as mice lacking the protein and human JEB patients with mutations in COL17A1, the open-reading frame encoding COL17, exhibit a premature aged skin phenotype, including gray hair and hair loss (Matsumura et al., 2016; Nishie et al., 2007; Tanimura et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Reduced labeling of epidermal basement membrane proteins, including COL17, in human skin has been associated with aging.
source: Additionally, reduced labeling of epidermal basement membrane proteins, including COL17, in human skin has been associated with aging (Langton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Neonatal IFE skin (P1, postnatal day 1) of Col17a1−/− mice showed transient epidermal hyperproliferation.
source: Neonatal IFE skin (P1, postnatal day 1) of Col17a1−/− mice showed transient epidermal hyperproliferation, as demonstrated by counting the epidermal layers and the numbers of epidermal cells and phospho-Histone H3 (PH3)-positive cells (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1a-b.

claim: The numbers of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA)- and Bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU)-positive cells in the Col17a1−/− IFE basal cells at P1 were increased compared with the controls.
source: The numbers of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA)- and Bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU)-positive cells in the Col17a1−/− IFE basal cells at P1 were also increased compared with the controls (Figure 1c), indicating that COL17 deletion affects both the S and M phases in the cell cycle of IFE neonatal keratinocytes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: COL17 deletion affects both the S and M phases in the cell cycle of IFE neonatal keratinocytes.
source: The numbers of proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA)- and Bromodeoxyuridine (BrdU)-positive cells in the Col17a1−/− IFE basal cells at P1 were also increased compared with the controls (Figure 1c), indicating that COL17 deletion affects both the S and M phases in the cell cycle of IFE neonatal keratinocytes.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the PCNA and BrdU data.

claim: The proliferative IFE phenotype of Col17a1−/− mice gradually waned postnatally, and the epidermal thickness and the number of PH3-positive cells became comparable with those of the controls at P20.
source: The proliferative IFE phenotype of Col17a1−/− mice gradually waned postnatally, and the epidermal thickness and the number of PH3-positive cells became comparable with those of the controls at P20 (Figure 1a–b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1a-b.

claim: The gene expression of Itga6 was increased in Col17a1−/− IFE skin.
source: The gene expression of Itga6, which might compensate for COL17 deficiency, was increased in Col17a1−/− IFE skin, whereas the expression of Itgb1, itgb4, lamb3 and lamc2 was not altered (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The expression of Itgb1, itgb4, lamb3 and lamc2 was not altered in Col17a1−/− IFE skin.
source: The gene expression of Itga6, which might compensate for COL17 deficiency, was increased in Col17a1−/− IFE skin, whereas the expression of Itgb1, itgb4, lamb3 and lamc2 was not altered (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The mRNA expression levels of Tgm1, Ppl and Ivl were somewhat higher in Col17a1−/− IFE skin.
source: The mRNA expression levels of Tgm1, Ppl and Ivl were somewhat higher in Col17a1−/− IFE skin (Figure 1d), while loricrin-labeled granular cell layers were not expanded in these mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Loricrin-labeled granular cell layers were not expanded in Col17a1−/− mice.
source: The mRNA expression levels of Tgm1, Ppl and Ivl were somewhat higher in Col17a1−/− IFE skin (Figure 1d), while loricrin-labeled granular cell layers were not expanded in these mice (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Dye-permeability and transepidermal water loss at day 18.5 of embryogenesis (E18.5) were comparable between the Col17a1−/− mice and the controls.
source: Dye-permeability and transepidermal water loss at day 18.5 of embryogenesis (E18.5) were comparable between the Col17a1−/− mice and the controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c), indicating that IFE keratinocyte differentiation was not greatly altered in Col17a1−/− skin.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: IFE keratinocyte differentiation was not greatly altered in Col17a1−/− skin.
source: Dye-permeability and transepidermal water loss at day 18.5 of embryogenesis (E18.5) were comparable between the Col17a1−/− mice and the controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b–c), indicating that IFE keratinocyte differentiation was not greatly altered in Col17a1−/− skin.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the dye-permeability and TEWL data.

claim: There was no increase in the number of cells positive for cleaved caspase-3, a marker of apoptosis, in the Col17a1−/− epidermis compared with the controls.
source: There was no increase in the number of cells positive for cleaved caspase-3, a marker of apoptosis, in the Col17a1−/− epidermis compared with the controls (Figure 1e).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The dermo-epidermal junction of the Col17a1−/− IFE presented hypoplastic hemidesmosomes.
source: The electron microscopy results indicated that the dermo-epidermal junction of the Col17a1−/− IFE presented hypoplastic hemidesmosomes in accordance with previous observations on the back skin of Col17a1−/− mice (Nishie et al., 2007) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: There were no significant differences in the number of inflammatory infiltrates, including CD3+, F4/80+ and Ly-6G+ cells, in the dermis of Col17a1−/− mice and control mice.
source: There were no significant differences in the number of inflammatory infiltrates, including CD3+, F4/80+ and Ly-6G+ cells, in the dermis of Col17a1−/− mice and control mice, which excludes inflammation as a contributor to immature hemidesmosome formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–g).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1e-g.

claim: Inflammation is excluded as a contributor to immature hemidesmosome formation in Col17a1−/− mice.
source: There were no significant differences in the number of inflammatory infiltrates, including CD3+, F4/80+ and Ly-6G+ cells, in the dermis of Col17a1−/− mice and control mice, which excludes inflammation as a contributor to immature hemidesmosome formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1e–g).
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the inflammatory cell data.

claim: An in silico model recapitulated the transient epidermal hyperproliferation of the Col17a1−/− neonatal IFE upon the loosening of the attachment of committed progenitor cells to the BMZ.
source: To explain the transient epidermal hyperproliferation of the Col17a1−/− neonatal IFE, we exploited an in silico model (Kobayashi et al., 2016) to recapitulate the epidermal development. As COL17 serves as a linker between the epidermis and dermis and is expressed in basal cells, most of which are committed progenitor cells in the epidermis (Doupé and Jones, 2012; Lim et al., 2013), epidermal thickness was calculated upon the loosening of the attachment of committed progenitor cells to the BMZ. In the model with diminished adhesion, the epidermal thickness was transiently increased and gradually returned to the baseline (Figure 1f), which was compatible with the experimental observations of Col17a1−/− neonates and with the transient hypertrophy of Itga6- and Itgb1-null epidermis (Brakebusch et al., 2000; Niculescu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by in silico modeling data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: COL17 deletion induces epidermal thickening by the hyperproliferation of IFE keratinocytes, at least partially through the loosening of dermo-epidermal adhesion at the neonatal stage.
source: These data suggest that COL17 deletion induces epidermal thickening by the hyperproliferation of IFE keratinocytes, at least partially through the loosening of dermo-epidermal adhesion at the neonatal stage.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the in silico modeling and experimental data.

claim: The cell proliferation rates of NHEKs treated with COL17A1 siRNAs were slightly decreased.
source: The cell proliferation rates of NHEKs treated with COL17A1 siRNAs were slightly decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d), which is compatible with reduced proliferation of cultured keratinocytes derived from Col17a1−/− mice (Tanimura et al., 2011), and the colony-forming abilities of these cells were similar to those of control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b-d.

claim: The colony-forming abilities of NHEKs treated with COL17A1 siRNAs were similar to those of control cells.
source: The cell proliferation rates of NHEKs treated with COL17A1 siRNAs were slightly decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–d), which is compatible with reduced proliferation of cultured keratinocytes derived from Col17a1−/− mice (Tanimura et al., 2011), and the colony-forming abilities of these cells were similar to those of control cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2e–f).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2e-f.

claim: The proliferation potential of Col17a1−/− IFE is dependent on in vivo conditions.
source: These data indicate that the proliferation potential of Col17a1−/− IFE is dependent on in vivo conditions.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: The expression levels of Wnt-related molecules (Fzd4, Nfatc2, Nfatc4 and Tcf7) were significantly decreased in Col17a1−/− neonatal IFE skin compared with controls.
source: The screening data showed that the expression levels of Wnt-related molecules (Fzd4, Nfatc2, Nfatc4 and Tcf7) were significantly decreased in Col17a1−/− neonatal IFE skin compared with controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR screening data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The TGF-β and p-Smad2 immunostaining in Col17a1−/− IFE keratinocytes was comparable with that in IFE cells in the controls.
source: Although the expression of some TGF-β−related genes was altered in Col17a1−/− IFE skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a), the TGF-β and p-Smad2 immunostaining in Col17a1−/− IFE keratinocytes was comparable with that in IFE cells in the controls, in contrast to the TGF-β and p-Smad2 reduction in Col17a1−/− HFSCs (Tanimura et al., 2011) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b–c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b-c.

claim: The expression levels of the Wnt target genes (Tcf7l1, Tcf7l2, and Axin2), the receptor gene (Fzd4), and stimulatory Wnt genes (Wnt2, Wnt2b, Wnt5a) were significantly downregulated in Col17a1−/− mice.
source: In line with the screening qPCR data, the expression levels of the Wnt target genes (Tcf7 l1, Tcf7 l2, and Axin2), the receptor gene (Fzd4), and stimulatory Wnt genes (Wnt2, Wnt2b, Wnt5a) were significantly downregulated in Col17a1−/−mice, whereas expression of the inhibitory Wnt gene (Wnt4) was increased (Figure 2a) (Bernard et al., 2008; Mikels and Nusse, 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Expression of the inhibitory Wnt gene (Wnt4) was increased in Col17a1−/− mice.
source: In line with the screening qPCR data, the expression levels of the Wnt target genes (Tcf7 l1, Tcf7 l2, and Axin2), the receptor gene (Fzd4), and stimulatory Wnt genes (Wnt2, Wnt2b, Wnt5a) were significantly downregulated in Col17a1−/−mice, whereas expression of the inhibitory Wnt gene (Wnt4) was increased (Figure 2a) (Bernard et al., 2008; Mikels and Nusse, 2006).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The number of basal cells positive for LEF1, a nuclear Wnt mediator of Wnt signaling, was reduced in neonatal Col17a1−/− mice IFE.
source: The changes in these genes were paralleled by a reduction of basal cells positive for LEF1, a nuclear Wnt mediator of Wnt signaling, in neonatal Col17a1−/− mice IFE (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The reduction in LEF1-positive basal cells was transient, and the number of LEF1-positive basal cells was comparable between the Col17a1−/− mice and the control mice at P4.
source: This reduction was also transient, and the number of LEF1-positive basal cells was comparable between the Col17a1−/− mice and the control mice at P4, which might account for the transient epidermal hyperproliferation of the paw IFE in Col17a1−/− mice.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The number of nuclear β-catenin-positive cells in Col17a1−/− mice IFE was diminished compared to the controls.
source: As β-catenin binds to LEF1 in the nucleus in the Wnt-canonical pathway (Lien and Fuchs, 2014), we performed β-catenin immunostaining. The number of nuclear β-catenin-positive cells in Col17a1−/− mice IFE was diminished compared to the controls (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Overexpression of human COL17 significantly upregulated Wnt activity in STF293 reporter cells.
source: To further evaluate the relationship between Wnt signaling and COL17, we utilized SuperTopFlash 293 (STF293) reporter cells (Tsukiyama et al., 2015). Overexpression of human COL17 significantly upregulated Wnt activity in this cell line (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by reporter assay data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The LacZ-positive area that was indicative of active Wnt signaling in the IFE was significantly diminished in the ins-Topgal+:Col17a1−/− mice.
source: Additionally, to visualize Wnt signaling in vivo, we crossed ins-Topgal+ mice (Moriyama et al., 2007) with Col17a1−/− mice. The LacZ-positive area that was indicative of active Wnt signaling in the IFE was significantly diminished in the ins-Topgal+:Col17a1−/− mice (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: COL17 expression stabilizes Wnt signaling.
source: These results suggest that COL17 expression stabilizes Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the reporter assay and in vivo Wnt signaling data.

claim: In JEB epidermis, the numbers of LEF1-positive cells and cells with nuclear β-catenin were decreased, while the number of PH3-positive cells was elevated.
source: To examine whether these findings correlate with the phenotype of JEB patients with COL17 deficiency, we also performed immunostainings for LEF1, β-catenin and PH3 in JEB skin. In the JEB epidermis, the numbers of LEF1-positive cells and cells with nuclear β-catenin were decreased, while the number of PH3-positive cells was elevated (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); these findings were compatible with the data from the Col17a1−/− mice, although this result requires further investigation due to the small sample size.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Neonatal K14-deltaNLef1 mice IFE exhibited epidermal thickening and a larger number of PH3-positive basal cells than the controls.
source: K14-deltaNLef1 mice express a Lef1 transgene that lacks a β-catenin-binding site under the control of the keratin 14 (K14) promoter and serve as a model of inactive Wnt signaling in the epidermis (Niemann et al., 2002). Neonatal K14-deltaNLef1 mice IFE exhibited epidermal thickening and a larger number of PH3-positive basal cells than the controls (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The number of BrdU- and PH3-positive epidermal cells was increased in mice treated with Wnt inhibitors (IWP-2 or Wnt-C59) at P1 compared with untreated control mice.
source: To confirm that the abated Wnt activities were related to neonatal IFE proliferation in vivo, we intraperitoneally administered Wnt inhibitors (IWP-2 or Wnt-C59) into wild-type mouse neonates (Kuo et al., 2016; Carotenuto et al., 2017). The number of BrdU- and PH3-positive epidermal cells was increased in mice treated with these inhibitors at P1 compared with untreated control mice (Figure 2g).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Transgenic rescue by the expression of human COL17 under the K14 promoter in Col17a1−/− mice abrogated IFE hyperproliferation and restored LEF1- and nuclear β-catenin-positive basal cells.
source: Transgenic rescue by the expression of human COL17 (hCOL17) under the K14 promoter in Col17a1−/− mice (Nishie et al., 2007) abrogated IFE hyperproliferation and restored LEF1- and nuclear β-catenin-positive basal cells (Figure 3a,c–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 3a, c-d.

claim: The expression levels of Wnt-related genes that were altered in Col17a1−/− mice at P1 were restored by transgenic rescue with hCOL17.
source: The expression levels of Wnt-related genes that were altered in Col17a1−/− mice at P1 were restored by transgenic rescue with hCOL17 (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: COL17 unambiguously contributes to the maintenance of neonatal IFE proliferation via its effect on Wnt signaling.
source: These data demonstrate that COL17 unambiguously contributes to the maintenance of neonatal IFE proliferation via its effect on Wnt signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the transgenic rescue data.

claim: In the IFE of aged mice, the epidermis was thickened, and the numbers of PH3-, BrdU- and PCNA-positive cells were increased.
source: We compared wild-type (WT) young mice (6 to 10 weeks old) with aged mice (19 to 27 months old). In the IFE of aged mice, the epidermis was thickened, and the numbers of PH3-, BrdU- and PCNA-positive cells were increased (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Physical aging leads to paw IFE hyperproliferation.
source: This phenomenon was specific to paw skin and was not observed in the back skin IFE (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), as was the case for the neonatal Col17a1−/− IFE. These data indicate that physical aging leads to paw IFE hyperproliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the aged mouse data.

claim: The gene expression levels of Itga6 and Itgb1 were decreased in the aged mouse IFE.
source: The gene expression levels of Itga6 and Itgb1 were decreased in the aged mouse IFE, whereas that of Col17a1 did not change (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The gene expression level of Col17a1 did not change in the aged mouse IFE.
source: The gene expression levels of Itga6 and Itgb1 were decreased in the aged mouse IFE, whereas that of Col17a1 did not change (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: The expression levels of differentiation markers (Tgm1, Ppl, and Evpl) were not greatly affected in aged mouse IFE.
source: Furthermore, the expression levels of differentiation markers (Tgm1, Ppl, and Evpl) were not greatly affected.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results.

claim: The distribution of COL17 was dramatically altered in the IFE of aged mice and humans.
source: Although Col17a1 gene expression was unaffected, the distribution of COL17 was dramatically altered in the IFE of aged mice and humans.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results.

claim: The apico-lateral portion of COL17 (non-hemidesmosomal COL17) was greatly reduced in the IFE of aged mice and humans.
source: The apico-lateral portion of COL17 (non-hemidesmosomal COL17) was greatly reduced in the IFE of aged mice and humans, as detected with antibodies targeting the extracellular portion of COL17 (Figure 4c) and is in line with the recent publication on age-related alterations of COL17 in human skin (Langton et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The altered COL17 distribution in aged IFE was also observed in the IFE of Klotho−/− mice, a premature aging model.
source: This phenomenon was also observed in the IFE of Klotho−/− mice, a premature aging model (Kuro-o, 2008).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The involvement of COL17 proteolytic cleavage (ectodomain shedding) in the altered COL17 distribution was excluded.
source: The involvement of COL17 proteolytic cleavage, so-called ectodomain shedding (Nishie et al., 2012, 2015), in the altered COL17 distribution was excluded using several antibodies that recognize the intracellular portions of COL17 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Triton X-100-treated young IFE lost the apico-lateral portion of COL17 and resembled the aged epidermis.
source: To confirm the depletion of non-hemidesmosomal COL17 in the aged IFE, the sections were treated with Triton X-100 prior to immunostaining (Hirako et al., 1998). In both mouse and human skin, Triton X-100-treated young IFE lost the apico-lateral portion of COL17 and resembled the aged epidermis (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: In 3D-reconstructed images, COL17 was confined to the basement membrane in the aged IFE, while basal cells of young mice had COL17 that was associated with the apical, lateral and basal membranes.
source: To further examine the reduction in the apico-lateral portion of COL17 in aged mice, we performed whole-mount staining of the IFE (Figure 4e). In 3D-reconstructed images, COL17 was confined to the basement membrane in the aged IFE, while basal cells of young mice had COL17 that was associated with the apical, lateral and basal membranes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by 3D imaging data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: COL17 was detected at the apico-lateral cell periphery of basal keratinocytes but did not co-localize with desmosomal proteins (desmogleins 1 and 2).
source: Using high-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) imaging on young WT mouse IFE (Figure 4f), COL17 was detected at the apico-lateral cell periphery of basal keratinocytes but did not co-localize with desmosomal proteins (desmogleins 1 and 2), indicating that the apico-lateral COL17 in basal keratinocytes was not incorporated into desmosomes, which are highly insoluble.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by SIM imaging data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: The apico-lateral COL17 in basal keratinocytes was not incorporated into desmosomes.
source: Using high-resolution structured illumination microscopy (SIM) imaging on young WT mouse IFE (Figure 4f), COL17 was detected at the apico-lateral cell periphery of basal keratinocytes but did not co-localize with desmosomal proteins (desmogleins 1 and 2), indicating that the apico-lateral COL17 in basal keratinocytes was not incorporated into desmosomes, which are highly insoluble.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the SIM imaging data.

claim: The distributions of integrins α6 and β1 were not modified by aging.
source: In contrast to COL17 dynamics with aging, the distributions of integrins α6 and β1 were not modified by aging (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4a.

claim: Other hemidesmosomal proteins (BP230 and Plectin) were unchanged with aging.
source: Other hemidesmosomal proteins (BP230 and Plectin) were also unchanged (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4b.

claim: Sustained Col17a1 gene expression in IFE skin contrasted with the decreased expression of many collagens and laminins with aging.
source: Sustained Col17a1 gene expression in IFE skin contrasted with the decreased expression of many collagens and laminins with aging (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c–d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4c-d.

claim: Physical aging leads to paw IFE hypertrophy and modifies COL17 distribution in the epidermis in a posttranslational manner.
source: These results suggest that physical aging leads to paw IFE hypertrophy and modifies COL17 distribution in the epidermis in a posttranslational manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the aging data.

claim: EDTA treatment eliminated apico-lateral COL17 in basal cells, while hemidesmosomal COL17 was present.
source: Because calcium distribution is changed in the aged epidermis (Denda et al., 2003) and the calcium concentration in the epidermis is lower in aged individuals than in young individuals (Rinnerthaler et al., 2015), whole IFE skin samples collected from young mice were treated with EDTA to simulate changes in calcium concentration in aged IFE. Whole mount staining showed that EDTA treatment eliminated apico-lateral COL17 in basal cells, while hemidesmosomal COL17 was present (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by whole mount staining data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The calcium concentration (or the concentrations of other molecules chelated by EDTA) may affect the COL17 distribution in the IFE.
source: This finding suggests that the calcium concentration (or the concentrations of other molecules chelated by EDTA) may affect the COL17 distribution in the IFE.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the EDTA treatment data.

claim: Phospho-aPKC, an active form of aPKC, was reduced in IFE with aging.
source: Among the numerous cellular events influenced by calcium dynamics, we focused on atypical protein kinase C (aPKC), a key regulator of epithelial polarity (Niessen et al., 2013). The expression levels of aPKCζ and aPKCλ/ι, aPKC isoforms expressed by basal epidermal cells are dependent on the calcium concentration in cultured keratinocytes (Helfrich et al., 2007), and the ablation of aPKCλ/ι in the epidermis leads to premature aging phenotypes, such as gray hair, hair loss and IFE thickening, closely resembling Col17a1−/− mice (Niessen et al., 2013; Osada et al., 2015). Phospho-aPKC, an active form of aPKC, was reduced in IFE with aging (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The axis of cell division in the aged IFE tended toward asymmetric cell division (ACD).
source: Consistent with this finding, the axis of cell division in the aged IFE tended toward asymmetric cell division (ACD) (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by cell division analysis data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The pharmacological inhibition of aPKC diminished the apico-lateral COL17 in basal cells.
source: To recapitulate aged skin with attenuated aPKC, we treated young mouse IFE samples with Go6983, a pan-PKC inhibitor, and myristoylated pseudosubstrate inhibitor (myr PSI), which is specific for aPKCζ and aPKCλ/ι (Gschwendt et al., 1996; Helfrich et al., 2007; Standaert et al., 1999). According to the whole mount staining, the pharmacological inhibition of aPKC diminished the apico-lateral COL17 in basal cells (Figure 5d–e).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by whole mount staining data shown in Figure 5d-e.

claim: EDTA treatment and aPKC inhibition diminished apico-lateral membranous COL17 in basal cells of reconstructed human 3D epidermis.
source: EDTA treatment and aPKC inhibition also diminished apico-lateral membranous COL17 in basal cells of reconstructed human 3D epidermis (Figure 5f–h).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by 3D epidermis data shown in Figure 5f-h.

claim: An aging-induced alteration of aPKC contributes to spatial changes in COL17 in the IFE.
source: These data indicate that an aging-induced alteration of aPKC contributes to spatial changes in COL17 in the IFE.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the aPKC inhibition data.

claim: There were no discernible changes between aged and young IFE skin in the expression levels of the proteases genes known to degrade COL17.
source: COL17 undergoes posttranslational modifications, such as ectodomain shedding and degradation, in physiological and pathological settings through the action of several proteases, such as disintegrin and metalloproteinases 9, 10, and 17 (ADAM9/10/17), matrix metalloproteinase-9 (MMP9), neutrophil elastase (ELANE) and other serine proteases (Hirako et al., 1998; Nishie, 2014). There were no discernible changes between aged and young IFE skin in the expression levels of the proteases genes known to degrade COL17 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by microarray data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5a.

claim: The involvement of MMP9 in COL17 degradation in aged IFE was excluded by the observation of the IFE in Serpine1−/− mice.
source: The involvement of MMP9 in COL17 degradation in aged IFE was further excluded by the observation of the IFE in Serpine1−/− mice, which lack plasminogen activator inhibitor-1, blocking MMP9 activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5b.

claim: ELANE was located along the BMZ of the IFE, an expression pattern different from that is seen in hair follicles and back skin.
source: ELANE, which degrades COL17 adjacent to HFSCs (Matsumura et al., 2016), was located along the BMZ of the IFE, an expression pattern different from that is seen in hair follicles and back skin (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5c.

claim: Physical aging did not affect ELANE labeling in the IFE.
source: Physical aging did not affect ELANE labeling in the IFE.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results.

claim: Proteases may not play major roles in the loss of apico-lateral COL17 in the IFE.
source: These data suggest that proteases may not play major roles in the loss of apico-lateral COL17 in the IFE.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the protease expression data.

claim: K14-hCOL17 transgenic mice showed COL17 on all surfaces of IFE basal cells at an age >19 months.
source: Next, we tested whether hCOL17 overexpression could reverse the aged IFE phenotype. K14-hCOL17 transgenic mice, which overexpress hCOL17 under the K14 promoter, showed COL17 on all surfaces of IFE basal cells at an age >19 months (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The epidermis was thinner, and the numbers of PH3- and PCNA-positive cells were reduced in the K14-hCOL17 aged IFE compared to the wild type.
source: In association with this observation, the epidermis was thinner, and the numbers of PH3- and PCNA-positive cells were reduced in the K14-hCOL17 aged IFE compared to the wild type (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: The expression levels of Itga6 and Itgb1 were similar in K14-hCOL17 aged IFE and age-matched controls.
source: However, the expression levels of Itga6 and Itgb1 were similar in K14-hCOL17 aged IFE and age-matched controls (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: COL17 might act downstream of Itga6 and Itgb1 stem cell markers and can keep the IFE in a juvenile state when overexpressed.
source: These data suggest that COL17 might act downstream of these stem cell markers and can keep the IFE in a juvenile state when overexpressed.
evidence: This is an inference stated in the results based on the K14-hCOL17 aged IFE data.

claim: Premature aged Col17a1−/− IFE (3 months old) exhibited epidermal thickening with an increased number of BrdU-positive basal cells.
source: Premature aged Col17a1−/− IFE (3 months old, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) exhibited epidermal thickening with an increased number of BrdU-positive basal cells, while the numbers of PCNA- or PH3-positive cells were comparable with age-matched controls (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The numbers of PCNA- or PH3-positive cells in premature aged Col17a1−/− IFE (3 months old) were comparable with age-matched controls.
source: Premature aged Col17a1−/− IFE (3 months old, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) exhibited epidermal thickening with an increased number of BrdU-positive basal cells, while the numbers of PCNA- or PH3-positive cells were comparable with age-matched controls (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by histological data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: There were no obvious alterations in Wnt-related molecules in the young adolescent IFE.
source: Unlike neonatal IFE hypertrophy via inactive Wnt signaling, there were no obvious alterations in Wnt-related molecules in the young adolescent IFE (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results and supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: COL17 overexpression suppresses epidermal hyperproliferation associated with physical aging in the IFE.
source: These results demonstrate that COL17 overexpression suppresses epidermal hyperproliferation associated with physical aging in the IFE.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the K14-hCOL17 aged IFE data.

claim: COL17 plays a central role in regulating interfollicular epidermis (IFE) proliferation.
source: Here, we show that COL17 plays a central role in regulating interfollicular epidermis (IFE) proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: COL17 is indispensable for regulating IFE proliferation in neonatal mice through activating the Wnt pathway.
source: We show that COL17 is indispensable for regulating IFE proliferation in neonatal mice through activating the Wnt pathway.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction.

claim: The IFE hyperproliferation is induced by organismal aging and can be reversed by COL17 replenishment.
source: The IFE hyperproliferation is induced by organismal aging and can be reversed by COL17 replenishment.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion stated in the introduction.
